title: Cheryl Lerena
dek: The verse of David's mother — some thirty poems, including a pandemic diary written in rhyme across two years.
living: **Cheryl Lerena is living.** This archive's rule for the living is **name only** — no dates, no places of residence, no photographs — and that rule is kept here. What is published is **her work**, at her son's request, and nothing about her life.
lead:
She is a **writer**, and the folder says so before a word is read: **eight book projects**, one redrafted **eleven times between 2005 and 2020**; a shelf of short stories; a writers' group, *The Write Company*, with its exercises and its poetry competition.

Most of the poems below come from a page **she assembled and titled herself** — *«Cheryl Anne Lerena Defranceski — Poems, Writings & Diary of a "Nutter"»* — where she introduces her own work in her own voice: *«this is another heartbreaking poem I wrote to him»*, *«so I wrote a poem»*. **This is her selection, not the archive's.**

The largest thing in it is a **pandemic diary in verse** — at least a dozen dated poems from March 2020 into 2021, ending in a death. It is the most sustained piece of writing she has left, and nobody had ever set it out in order.

poems.title: A poem for our grandchild
poems.occasion: Dated **13 August 2016**, and the fullest version names him: *«A POEM FOR OUR GRANDCHILD **(Alessio)** – by Cheryl Anne Defranceski»*. **Alessio was born the following March.** The only piece in the whole folder where she signs herself as the author of a poem.
text: We have not met you ….. yet
to see if you're a boy or girl
to count your fingers and your toes
and feel the softness of your nose
to touch your skin and hear your cries
and smell the sweetness of your flesh
to gaze deep in your eyes
and whisper softly in your ears
our endless love for you always
And as we wait with bated breath
for you who we have not yet met
sleep well sweet child until it's time
for you to safely leave the womb
We wait for you with bated breath …..
poems.note: Fifteen lines that never once say *I*. It is **«we»** all the way through, and almost every line is a **sense** — touch, hearing, smell, sight. A poem about a person who does not exist yet, written entirely out of what it will be like to have a body near you.

poems.title: Deda Baba
poems.occasion: Her own note above it: *«My grandson Alessio calls me Baba or Babi and Ivan Deda. He thinks of the two of us as one. So I wrote a poem.»*
text: In the eyes of a child we are one
In the eyes of a child we are one
In the eyes of a child we are one
poems.note: The two names run together into one word — **DedaBabaDedaBaba** — and it beats. *lubdub* is a heartbeat written down. A child's mispronunciation turned into a poem about a marriage, and the marriage vow — *till death us do part* — dropped in the middle of it without ceremony.

poems.title: The mouse in the house
poems.occasion: Her note: *«written for Alessio about the mouse they discovered who was eating all the vegetables they were growing»* — **21 July 2020**, in the middle of the Corona sequence.
text: And there was a mouse…… eeeeekkkkk
I need to eat your beet
poems.note: Written in the same month as *«Sick always sick»*, for a three-year-old, in the same rhyming scheme she was using on the virus. **The mouse wins the argument.**

poems.title: Forever
poems.occasion: Her own note: *«After moving from Durban to Johannesburg, Ivan and I still had interference and were tormented still trying to be together where we belonged. This is another heartbreaking poem I wrote to him in this tumultuous time.»* Signed **«From 'Muffet' to I.D. with love»**.
poems.conf: doc — introduced and signed by her
text: To you I give not myself
But my son, the one and only
I will shed many a tear
Keep him safe, happy and secure
You will be in my heart
My heart belongs to you forever
Say I do not love you
Sweet happy memories I will cherish
Of all the wonderful happy moments
I will hold dear in my heart forever
poems.note: **«To you I give not myself / But my son»** is one of the hardest first lines in the whole collection, and she never explains it. The pet names at the foot — *Muffet*, *I.D.* — are the only signature.

poems.title: Sitting at Café Bon-Bon in Bedfordview
poems.occasion: Undated. Her own heading gives the café and the suburb.
poems.note: A poem written **at a table in a coffee shop**, and it says so in its title. *«Memories that flood / Like the drawing of blood»* is the image the poem is built on — memory as something drawn out of you by a needle, against your will.

poems.title: Two sides
text: That life has not one but two sides
Then the dark cold of night
That life has not one but two sides
Hear the laughter loud and clear
That life has not one but two sides
Taste the words of kindness and love
Spit out the words of lies and hate
That life has not one but two sides
Smell the sweetness of a rose
and the stench of a titan arum
That life has not one but two sides
To the tale of two sides
To the tale of two sides
poems.note: The most **built** thing she wrote. A refrain five times over, and behind it a structure she never announces: **the five senses in order** — sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch. For its stink she reaches past the obvious and picks a **titan arum**, the corpse flower, which is somebody who went looking. The close swaps *eyes* for **ears**.

poems.title: A heart breaks
poems.note: Seventeen lines, none longer than four words, running a single night into a day and back to sunset. The only thing that develops is the pain: it *eats*, and then it **feasts**. And the heart is never *hers* — never *my* heart, always ***a*** heart.

poems.title: I had a darling sister
poems.occasion: Written for the **first anniversary** of her sister Rene's death and read to the family. **Catherine Tersia Lerena, 21 May 1952 – 30 September 1999.** It stands inside a memorial address, not set apart as verse — which is why nobody had ever seen it as a poem.
poems.conf: doc — signed at the foot of the document it stands in
text: A dream her life was not
She knew pain as her friend
poems.note:
Nine lines, no rhyme, ending on an ellipsis rather than a full stop — the same trailing dots she uses all through the prose around it, as though the sentence could not be finished. **«She knew pain as her friend»** is the line it turns on. It is not a comfort and it does not try to be.

**Two sisters, twenty-two years apart, and a poem for each.**

poems.title: If love could change the way things are
poems.occasion: Stands a few paragraphs below «I had a darling sister», in the same memorial address.
text: If love could change the way things are
You would live forever and go so far
You'd know that I am always there
That I'll always love you, I'll always care
poems.note: Four lines rhymed **aabb**, immediately before the sentence *«In October of 1992 a card arrived in the mail … here it is, I will share it with you»*. It may be hers, or it may be the verse off that card. The document does not say, and this archive will not decide for it.

excluded.heading: Two poems that are not hers, and are not printed
excluded.text:
**«Life is a sojourn here on earth»** sits in a letter she wrote to her surviving sister in **November 1999**, six weeks after Rene died. It is by **Helen Steiner Rice**, the American writer of devotional verse whose poems went out on greeting cards by the million — almost certainly how it reached a Johannesburg letterbox. **In copyright. Not printed.**

**«Each day I love you more, today more than yesterday and less than tomorrow»** is a single line kept in the Poems folder. It is a translation of **Rosemonde Gérard**, *L'éternelle chanson*, 1889 — *«chaque jour je t'aime davantage, aujourd'hui plus qu'hier et bien moins que demain»* — one of the most quoted lines in French. **Not hers either.**

Both are named rather than dropped in silence, because **a woman keeping a poem she loves is not the author of it**, and an archive that prints everything in a folder ends up attributing greeting cards to grieving people.

rest.heading: What else is in the folder, and why none of it is here
rest.text:
The poems are the smallest part of it. Also in the folder: **eight book projects** — *My Love Story*, redrafted eleven times from 2005 to 2020; *Husky*; *Soul Mates*; *A Murder*; *Desperate End*, whose first chapter was written for a creative-writing course and carries her name on the title; *Infidelity*; *Insanity*. Around **fifteen short stories**. Personal essays. A **writers' group** file thick with exercises, character sketches and competition entries.

**None of it is published**, and none of it is quoted here.

And a warning that has to be given plainly. **Several files in the Poems folder are not poems.** They are private prose, and some of it is about named living people — including her son — written in distress and never meant for a website. This archive has read them only far enough to know they are not verse, and has **published nothing from them, quoted nothing from them, and will not.**

If more of the writing is to appear, **it is Cheryl's to release, piece by piece.** This page will take whatever she gives it.

source: From the family's own writing folder, read 10 September 2026 at David's request. Poems transcribed exactly: line breaks, spelling, and the trailing ellipses are hers and are not corrected. «I had a darling sister» and «If love could change the way things are» come from the memorial address for Catherine Tersia Lerena, first anniversary, September 2000. Attributions for the two excluded poems: Helen Steiner Rice, and Rosemonde Gérard's «L'éternelle chanson», 1889. «My Gratitude Jar for the Year 2021» supplied in full by David, 10 September 2026, and quoted selectively.

pending.heading: A note on how this text was recovered
pending.text:
Her own compilation exists as a **screen capture**, not a document — three tall images with no text layer. The poems above were recovered by **optical character recognition** and then read back against the Word originals wherever both survive.

That means **small errors are possible**: a *«blowth»* that might be *«blow»*, an *«a physis»* that is almost certainly something else. Line breaks follow the capture. Where a reading looked wrong it was checked against the original file; where no original exists, the OCR stands and **may need her correction**.

Two poems — *«Gratefulness for 1 year»* and part of the Corona sequence — remain in **Apple Pages** format, whose text is compressed inside a binary this archive cannot decode. They need an export.

corona.heading: Corona — a diary in verse, 2020–2021
corona.intro:
She gave the sequence an acrostic, and the acrostic is the argument:

**C**apturing · **O**ur · **R**evelation **o**f · **N**ecessary · **A**cts

What follows is dated like a diary and rhymed like a nursery rhyme, and the pairing is the whole effect: *cobra* against *corona*, *sleaze* against *sneeze*, *blowth* — a word she appears to have made — against *cough*. **The lightness is not levity.** It is somebody rhyming her way through two years, and the rhymes hold until the last poem, when they stop mattering.
corona.close: The sequence turns in **May 2020** — *«Around the corner / Liberty peeks»* — and turns back. By **July** the rhymes are gone from the middle of the lines and the poems are lists: *«Sick always sick / Cough splutter / Sniffle snuffle»*. **Then it stops being about the world.**

elegy.heading: And then it took her sister
elegy.intro:
The last poems of the sequence are not about a pandemic. They are about one death in it — a sister she calls **«the older one, the wiser one»**, and elsewhere **«the Matriarch of our tribe»**, taken in the early hours of a Sunday morning.

She wrote her sister's **whole life** first, in rhymed couplets, from a girl on a bicycle to a family of thirteen — and only then let the disease into the poem.

poems.date: Her sister's life, and its end
text: Cold and bold he seized your life
poems.note:
Thirty-seven lines, and **thirty-four of them are a life being lived**. The disease gets three. The couplets are cheerful — *merry / berry*, *dedicated / celebrated* — right up to *«Cold and bold he seized your life»*, where the rhyme lands inside the line instead of at the end of it and the poem stops.

She signs it: ***«To my dearest sister, the older one, the wiser one, you will be forever missed and loved to infinity and beyond from your heartbroken sister Che.»***

text: How could you take her life
Like a thief in the night
poems.note: The rhyme survives four lines and then abandons her. **«Scared and alone / Fighting for breath»** is the only place in thirty poems where she says what the dying was actually like, and it is six words long. What is left at the end is not verse at all — *«I hate you parasite / Perish you murderer / Suffocate and die»* — a woman swearing at a virus.

text: Like a panther creeping on its prey
Seeking out a host to infect

dark.heading: One more, which she introduces herself
dark.text:
Among the poems she chose to publish is one she prefaces with a single line: ***«This is my translation of how I felt when the end was nearing.»***

It is printed here because **she printed it**, and because a collection of somebody's poems that quietly drops the darkest one is not their collection any more.
text2: Drawing in an ocean of tears
Vision clouds as thoughts flow through poisoned veins
As the misery of yesterday slips into a tunnel of oblivion
Light seeps as the nothingness arrives
dark.note:
No rhyme, no metre, and the longest lines she ever wrote. It moves in one direction only — from *screams* to *numbness* to *nothingness* — and the verbs turn passive as it goes, until the last thing that acts is not her. **«Death lusts»** is two words and it is the middle of the poem.

It is the only poem here with a **reader** in mind: she calls it a *translation*, as though the feeling were a language somebody else would need help with.

jar.heading: My Gratitude Jar for the Year 2021
jar.intro:
A **third form**, and the one that turns out to hold the key to the elegies. Three hundred and sixty-five numbered slots, one line each, kept through 2021. She heads it with a list rather than a sentence:

> *Gratitude is attitude. Believe, receive, forgive, respect, heal, connect, feel, soul, truth, love, peace, purpose, harmony*

Most of it is small on purpose — that is the form. *«Rainy days.» «Waking each morning.» «Clean house.» «Good coffees.»* Her husband recurs as a running joke with three names: **«my indispensable Sous Chef»**, **«my in-house hairdresser — my man — PRICELESS!!!»**, and simply **«my Man who works hard in the garden»**. On two days in March she gives up on sentences altogether and writes one word: **«MEMORIES.»** **«FRIENDSHIPS.»**

shape.heading: The shape of it says more than the entries
shape.text:
She filled **180 of 365 days — forty-nine per cent** — and the pattern of the blanks is the year.

**January is complete.** Thirty-one days out of thirty-one, the resolve of a new jar. Then it thins to thirteen or fourteen a month and stays there.

**Except June.** June jumps back to nineteen — the fullest month since January — and June is the month her sister died. **She wrote more in the worst month of the year**, and what she wrote in it was gratitude.

And then: **December is empty.** Not thin — empty. The jar's last entry is **25 November**, and it is *«Chats with Dainis reminiscing about our beloved Nita.»* She never picks it up again. **The year does not end; it stops.**

june.heading: June
june.text: The entries around her sister's death are the reason this document matters to the archive as well as to the reading of it.
rows: **«That Nita did not suffer — her death came quick.»**
**«Alessio for his wise words "Babi I'll send an angel to heaven to bring your sister back".»**
«All the family and friends who attended Nita's memorial service (even with Covid)»
«To the Lerena family for attending Nita's memorial service, and Robert's kind words»
«Chats with Dainis reminiscing about our beloved Nita»  — *the last entry in the jar*
june.close:
**6 June 2021 was a Sunday.** The Corona elegy opens *«Then without warning / Early hours Sunday morning»* — and the sequence, the jar and the calendar agree. The sister of *«the older one, the wiser one»*, *«the Matriarch of our tribe»*, is **Jeanette Riekstins, born Lerena, called Nita**, and she died on Sunday **6 June 2021**.

That is a fact this archive did not have an hour ago, and it came out of **a gratitude journal**.

jar.quiet: What is not printed here is most of it. The jar names **living people** — a daughter-in-law, grandchildren, cousins, friends, an aunt, a hairdresser, a roofer — and it records **their surgeries, their test results and their falls** alongside the weather. Those entries are hers and theirs. **The form is published; the file is not.**
